rows.title: A conserved zinc-finger gene BmZFO721 regulates meiosis and female fertility in silkworm, Bombyx mori.
rows.query: ((magnesium OR zinc OR "vitamin D" OR cobalamin OR "vitamin B12" OR folate OR iron OR selenium OR iodine) AND (deficiency OR supplementation OR cognition OR fatigue OR mood OR sleep)) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: A conserved zinc-finger gene BmZFO721 regulates meiosis and female fertility in silkworm, Bombyx mori.
rows.focus: Accurate meiotic progression during oogenesis is fundamental to oocyte maturation and female fertility in sexually reproducing organisms. In lepidopteran insects, however, the upstream regulators governing female meiotic progression, particularly ovary-specific functional genes, remain largely uncharacterized, and their in vivo roles in oocyte development are poorly understood. Here, we identified a gene encoding an ovary-specific C2H2-type zinc-finger protein (ZFP), designated BmZFO721 (Bombyx mori Zinc-Finger Ovary gene 721). Phylogenetic and genomic synteny analyses reveal that BmZFO721 is highly conserved across lepidopteran insects, and hybridization chain reaction staining demonstrates its specific expression in germ cells (nurse cells and oocytes) within ovarioles, with no detectable signal in somatic follicle cells or the germarium. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of BmZFO721 severely disrupts oogenesis, impairing synaptonemal complex (SC) assembly and chromosomal condensation. The synapsis deficiency triggers meiotic checkpoint activation and subsequent germ cell apoptosis, which eliminates aberrant oocytes and ultimately results in complete female sterility. In addition, transcriptomic analysis further suggests that the oogenic defects in mutants are associated with dysregulation of genes involved in DNA metabolism, chromatin structural organization, and nucleosome dynamics. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that BmZFO721 functions as a crucial regulator of meiotic progression and germ cell survival, revealing unique regulatory strategies in lepidopteran oogenesis.

rows.title: Selenium deficiency induces PANoptosis in porcine myocardial tissue via Sirt3-mediated YME1L1 acetylation under oxidative stress.
rows.query: ((magnesium OR zinc OR "vitamin D" OR cobalamin OR "vitamin B12" OR folate OR iron OR selenium OR iodine) AND (deficiency OR supplementation OR cognition OR fatigue OR mood OR sleep)) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Selenium deficiency induces PANoptosis in porcine myocardial tissue via Sirt3-mediated YME1L1 acetylation under oxidative stress.
rows.focus: Insufficient intake of the essential trace element selenium can lead to cardiovascular disease through oxidative stress. The expression of Sirtuin 3 (Sirt3)/YME1-like 1 ATPase (YME1L1) deacetylase pathway related factors is highly sensitive to intracellular redox fluctuations. However, its functional role in selenium‑deficient (-Se) myocardial tissue remains unclear. A porcine model of selenium deficiency was established by feeding a diet containing 0.030 mg/kg selenium. To investigate the role of YME1L1 acetylation, YME1L1‑K237R and YME1L1‑K237Q plasmids were transfected into cardiomyocytes. Oxidative stress, myocardial structure, mitochondrial morphology, protein acetylation, and PANoptosis markers were evaluated using histology, transmission electron microscopy, immunoprecipitation, western blot, and qRT‑PCR. Selenium deficiency induced oxidative stress, which downregulated Sirt3 and increased YME1L1 acetylation at K237, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction characterized by impaired mitochondrial dynamics, reduced ATP production, and mtDNA release. The deacetylation‑mimetic YME1L1‑K237R mutant significantly rescued PANoptosis. These findings identify an oxidative stress‑mediated Sirt3/YME1L1 acetylation axis, with YME1L1‑K237 as the critical acetylation switch, as a novel driver of PANoptosis in selenium‑deficient myocardium, offering new insights into the cardiac function of selenium.

rows.title: Comparative genomic insights into strain-specific zinc-promoting effects of the spore-forming probiotic Heyndrickxia coagulans.
rows.query: ((probiotic OR prebiotic OR synbiotic OR microbiome OR psychobiotic) AND (IBS OR "irritable bowel" OR anxiety OR depression OR sleep OR stress OR cognition)) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Comparative genomic insights into strain-specific zinc-promoting effects of the spore-forming probiotic Heyndrickxia coagulans.
rows.focus: Zinc deficiency is a prevalent micronutrient disorder, and probiotic intervention has emerged as a promising strategy to improve zinc bioavailability. However, the strain-specific characteristics and genetic basis underlying the zinc-promoting effects of probiotics remain poorly understood. Therefore, this study aimed to identify the key physiological properties and functional genes associated with the zinc-promoting capacity of Heyndrickxia coagulans (H. coagulans, formerly Bacillus coagulans). A Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cell monolayer model and a zinc-deficient mouse model were established to evaluate the zinc-promoting effects of H. coagulans. Male BALB/c mice were fed a zinc-deficient diet and orally administered H. coagulans spores (107 CFU per mouse per day) combined with zinc gluconate (0.15 mg Zn per mouse per day) for 4 weeks. Serum zinc concentration, alkaline phosphatase activity, organ indices, and intestinal zinc homeostasis-related gene expression were evaluated. Furthermore, comparative genomic analysis was performed to identify candidate genomic features potentially associated with strain-dependent differences in zinc-promoting capacity. Among the tested strains, H. coagulans CCFM1539, CCFM1540, and CCFM1541 exhibited distinct zinc-promoting capacities. In vitro, CCFM1539 significantly enhanced zinc transmembrane transport and modulated the transcription of zinc transporter genes. In vivo, supplementation with H. coagulans spores combined with zinc gluconate more effectively restored serum zinc concentration, alkaline phosphatase activity, organ indices, and intestinal zinc homeostasis-related gene expression (Zip4, Znt1, Znt2, and Vdr) than zinc supplementation alone. Notably, CCFM1541 showed the strongest overall zinc-promoting phenotype, with superior restoration of serum zinc concentration and Vdr expression. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that strain-specific zinc-promoting effects were associated with genes involved in ion transport, stress adaptation, carbohydrate metabolism, and cellular regulation. Among the CCFM1541-specific genes, ABC transporter-related genes, particularly gsiB, gsiC, gsiD, oppD, and oppF, were identified as candidate genes potentially associated with its superior zinc-promoting phenotype. In conclusion, the zinc-promoting effects of H. coagulans are strain-specific and are associated with changes in intestinal zinc homeostasis and bacterial genomic features. These findings provide genomic insights into probiotic-mediated mineral bioavailability and identify candidate genes for future functional validation.

rows.title: Systemic inflammation, gut microbiome composition, and cognitive performance among older Ugandans with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias: A cross-sectional study.
rows.query: ((probiotic OR prebiotic OR synbiotic OR microbiome OR psychobiotic) AND (IBS OR "irritable bowel" OR anxiety OR depression OR sleep OR stress OR cognition)) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Systemic inflammation, gut microbiome composition, and cognitive performance among older Ugandans with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias: A cross-sectional study.
rows.focus: Systemic inflammation is implicated in neurodegeneration; however, evidence linking circulating inflammatory biomarkers to cognitive decline remains inconsistent, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) is a standard systemic inflammatory marker; however, its relationship with cognitive performance and gut microbiome composition in sub-Saharan Africa remains underexplored. We investigated the association between hs-CRP and cognitive performance across older Ugandans diagnosed with Alzheimer disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and cognitively intact controls and examined whether gut microbial composition modified this relationship. We conducted a cross-sectional study of community-dwelling older adults in Wakiso District, Uganda. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Education-Adjusted Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Systemic inflammation was quantified using plasma hs-CRP, and gut microbial profiles were generated via full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multivariable linear regression models were used to evaluate the associations between log-transformed hs-CRP concentrations and MoCA scores, adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index. Linear regression assumptions were formally tested. Exploratory analyses examined taxon-level differential abundance across diagnostic categories, hs-CRP-microbiome correlations, and hs-CRP × taxon interaction terms on MoCA scores, with multiple-testing adjustment using the false discovery rate. The analytic cohort comprised 85 participants (mean age 77.5 ± 9.2 years; 67 AD, 10 MCI, and 8 controls). Median hs-CRP was higher in AD (1.96 [0.25-3.75] mg/L) than in MCI (0.25 [0.25-2.73] mg/L) and controls (0.25 [0.25-0.84] mg/L). Higher hs-CRP showed a modest inverse trend with MoCA scores that was not statistically significant after adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index (standardized , ). Advancing age was independently associated with poorer cognitive performance (standardized , ). Several microbial genera exhibited nominal differences across diagnostic groups and hs-CRP levels; however, no individual taxon-level associations or hs-CRP × microbiome interaction terms survived false discovery rate correction (). Circulating hs-CRP was not independently associated with global cognitive performance in this cohort of older Ugandans. Genus-level microbiome analyses yielded exploratory, hypothesis-generating patterns that warrant validation in larger longitudinal cohorts investigating gut-brain axis interactions in African populations.

rows.title: Kratom-labeled Products in the US Compared With Traditionally Consumed Natural Kratom in Southeast Asia.
rows.query: (kratom OR mitragynine OR "7-hydroxymitragynine" OR tianeptine OR phenibut OR "novel psychoactive" OR "opioid withdrawal" OR "benzodiazepine withdrawal") AND 2015:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Kratom-labeled Products in the US Compared With Traditionally Consumed Natural Kratom in Southeast Asia.
rows.focus: Kratom-labeled products consumed in the United States and natural kratom consumed in Southeast Asia (SEA) are very different in their chemistry and safety profiles. Water-based decoction, frequently consumed in SEA, is prepared using freshly harvested, not dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa tree, indigenous to the SEA region. Our research demonstrates that the decoction contains mitragynine and its congeners in organic, water-soluble salts form, not in the pure base alkaloids form. In addition, our preliminary evaluation has not detected 7-hydroxymitragynine, a highly potent oxidative derivative of mitragynine, in the decoction prepared from the freshly harvested and unprocessed leaves. The differences in the products' chemistry may be responsible for the observed differences in safety profiles between the products consumed in the United States and in the SEA countries. Kratom-labeled products in the United States are sold under the false promises that they reflect the natural kratom products consumed in SEA. Consumers of these products and health care practitioners in the United States may not be aware that the natural kratom products traditionally consumed in SEA (ie, freshly harvested unprocessed whole leaves and a water-based decoction prepared from such leaves) have different chemistry and are consumed differently than the US products, including kratom-leaf-derived US products (ie, capsules, powders, or tea bags claiming to contain dried natural kratom leaves), as well as the highly concentrated or semisynthetic products. The traditional natural products consumed in the SEA countries may also have a different safety profile and pharmacological effects.

rows.title: Nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase directly couples redox homeostasis to proline biosynthesis in human glioma.
rows.query: ((creatine[Title] OR "coenzyme Q10"[Title] OR CoQ10[Title] OR carnitine[Title] OR riboflavin[Title] OR nicotinamide[Title] OR "alpha lipoic acid"[Title]) AND (mitochondrial[Title/Abstract] OR fatigue[Title/Abstract] OR energy[Title/Abstract] OR exercise[Title/Abstract])) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase directly couples redox homeostasis to proline biosynthesis in human glioma.
rows.focus: Cancer cell proliferation requires a precise balance between biomass production and nutrient catabolism. The pyridine nucleotide cofactors nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide NAD(H) and NAD phosphate NADP(H) are central to this process, but their compartment-specific regulation is incompletely understood. Using in vivo isotope-labeled metabolite tracing in an orthotopic xenograft model, we find that human gliomas extensively synthesize proline, an amino acid previously associated with hypoxia tolerance. In glioma cells, we identify a hypoxia-enhanced proliferative sensitivity to environmental proline dependent on NADH to NADPH transhydrogenation from a spatially compartmentalized mitochondrial pool by the enzyme nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT). We demonstrate NNT-dependent generation of mitochondrial NADPH is important for proline accumulation, maintenance of antioxidant systems, and reductive metabolism in hypoxic glioma cells in vitro and tumor progression in vivo. Collectively, these results highlight proline accumulation as a marker of mitochondrial NAD(P)(H) homeostasis and NNT as a specific metabolic dependency in human glioma.

rows.title: Panax-derived Zingibroside R1 exerts allelopathic effects on root architecture by modulating the auxin transport pathway and oxidative stress responses.
rows.query: (ashwagandha OR "Withania somnifera" OR rhodiola OR ginseng OR "Panax ginseng" OR bacopa OR "Hericium erinaceus" OR "lion's mane" OR curcumin OR ganoderma) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Panax-derived Zingibroside R1 exerts allelopathic effects on root architecture by modulating the auxin transport pathway and oxidative stress responses.
rows.focus: The triterpenoid-rich Panax spp. possess notable allelopathic capabilities, yet current knowledge lacks comprehensive understanding of the biological mechanisms underlying these inhibitory effects. Here, we show that zingibroside R1 (ZR1), a newly identified allelochemical from Panax spp., inhibits the adventitious root growth in ginseng and primary root elongation in Arabidopsis. Mechanistic analyses revealed that ZR1 disrupts auxin transport, as evidenced by monitoring DR5::GFP and PINs markers. The effect of ZR1 on auxin transport was further elucidated through synergistic effects observed with the auxin transport inhibitor NPA and in the auxin transport mutants aux1 and pin2. Additionally, ZR1 downregulates key root development regulators, including stem cell maintenance regulators PLT1/2, WOX5, SHR, and SCR. Transcriptomic and biochemical data indicate that ZR1 triggers an ROS response in plants, which disrupts ROS scavenging-via altered peroxidase activities and reduced glutathione/oxidized glutathione balance-thereby impairing detoxification function and resulting in root shortening by regulation of auxin distribution and stem cell gene expression. Our results establish a mechanistic framework for understanding how ginsenosides mediate allelopathic effects on root development.

rows.title: Curcumin-Loaded Nanospheres Attenuate Fine Dust (PM(10))-Induced Cellular Toxicity by Suppressing Reactive Oxygen Species-Dependent Signaling in Human Keratinocytes.
rows.query: (ashwagandha OR "Withania somnifera" OR rhodiola OR ginseng OR "Panax ginseng" OR bacopa OR "Hericium erinaceus" OR "lion's mane" OR curcumin OR ganoderma) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Curcumin-Loaded Nanospheres Attenuate Fine Dust (PM10)-Induced Cellular Toxicity by Suppressing Reactive Oxygen Species-Dependent Signaling in Human Keratinocytes.
rows.focus: Curcumin has various biological effects, but its poor aqueous solubility limits its practical use. This study investigated the effects of curcumin-loaded nanospheres (CN) on cellular injury induced by fine dust (PM10) in HaCaT human keratinocytes and examined the signaling mechanisms involved. PM10 exposure significantly decreased cell viability, whereas CN at 10-4 μg/mL significantly restored cell viability and showed a protective effect at a lower concentration than unformulated curcumin. PM10 rapidly increased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, followed by activation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB). CN reduced ROS generation and inhibited activation of these signaling molecules. CN also restored the altered Bax/Bcl-2 balance, decreased caspase-3 cleavage, and reduced caspase-1-dependent IL-1β processing in PM10-exposed cells. Treatment with NAC and inhibitors of ERK, p38 MAPK, NF-κB, and caspase-1 further reduced PM10-induced cytotoxic and inflammatory responses, supporting the involvement of these pathways. Overall, CN attenuated fine dust-induced cellular toxicity in keratinocytes by suppressing ROS-dependent MAPK/NF-κB signaling and downstream apoptotic and inflammatory responses.

rows.title: Vitamin B12 replacement strategies: a Brazilian delphi consensus.
rows.query: ((magnesium OR zinc OR "vitamin D" OR cobalamin OR "vitamin B12" OR folate OR iron OR selenium OR iodine) AND (deficiency OR supplementation OR cognition OR fatigue OR mood OR sleep)) AND 2018:2026[pdat] AND hasabstract[text]
rows.verified_title: Vitamin B12 replacement strategies: a Brazilian delphi consensus.
rows.focus: Vitamin B12 deficiency is common in older adults, atrophic gastritis, and after bariatric surgery, and can cause irreversible neurological injury. Oral, sublingual, and intramuscular routes all correct serum concentrations, yet whether any route is superior for clinically meaningful outcomes is unclear, and international guidelines diverge. This consensus was convened to define where evidence is adequate, where it is lacking, and the priority research questions. This was a modified Delphi consensus study. The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method was applied through a two-stage process of 2 electronic rounds and an in-person meeting in São Paulo, Brazil. Panellists were recruited between 1 July 2025 and 15 July 2025. Thirty statements were voted on, presented as 31 graded items, using a binary (agree or disagree) format with a priori percentage-agreement grades (A+, 100%; A, 90%-99.9%; B, 80%-89.9%; C, 70%-79.9%; and D, 66%-69.9%). Draft statements, informed by a systematic review, were rated anonymously by a Brazilian multidisciplinary panel of 20 experts across haematology, gastroenterology, endocrinology, bariatric surgery, and geriatric medicine/neurology. Of 20 experts invited, all 20 agreed to participate and completed the electronic rounds (100%); 16 (80%) attended the in-person meeting. Patient representatives (n = 2) participated as non-voting observers. Grade A (at least 90% agreement) was the stopping rule. This consensus was not registered. In total, 30 statements across 6 modules were agreed, comprising 31 separately graded items as statement 1 was presented in two parts (1a and 1b); 22 of 31 items (71%) reached grade A+ (100% agreement) and 9 of 31 (29%) reached grade A (90%-99.9%). All routes were judged capable of normalising serum vitamin B12, but none showed proven superiority for symptom resolution, neurological recovery, functional status, or quality of life. Evidence gaps were greatest after bariatric surgery, in older adults with cognitive impairment or frailty, and in pernicious anaemia. Dosing, monitoring, and response definitions varied substantially. Vitamin B12 replacement across all routes remains guided primarily by biochemical rather than clinical evidence. Treatment should be individualised by aetiology, patient preference, feasibility, and access, with functional biomarkers and clinical assessment complementing serum levels. Adequately powered, long-term comparative trials using standardised, patient-centred outcomes are the priority. This work was funded by Myralis Indústria Farmacêutica Ltda, São Paulo, Brazil.
